title: Battles in the Supreme Court -- Ch. 10: BATTLES OVER CIVIL RIGHTS
keywords: there are really no illegitimate children; there are only illegitimate parents
consensuality of a contract of sale
primary_topics: Chapter 10 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' -- two civil-rights battles fought on the terrain of private law: the successional rights of natural children by legal fiction in De Santos v. Angeles, and the enforceability of a right of first refusal in Equatorial Realty v. Mayfair Theater

His dissent in De Santos: reading Articles 89, 269 and 270 of the Civil Code together, he argued that a natural child by legal fiction already satisfies the first two requisites of legitimation, so the subsequent valid marriage of the parents legitimates such a child as fully as an acknowledged natural child

The moral core of that dissent -- that children bear no fault for the marital impediments of their parents and should benefit by every intendment of the law: 'there are really no illegitimate children; there are only illegitimate parents'

His Separate Concurring Opinion in Mayfair: although a right of first refusal is normally not enforceable by specific performance, the contractual covenant here, the misdirected offer to Equatorial, and Mayfair's prompt suit for specific performance supplied presumed consent, so consensuality was satisfied and the sale could be rescinded
sub_topics: The taxonomy of filiation: the Family Code recognizes only legitimate and illegitimate children, while the Civil Code before August 3, 1988 further divided illegitimates into natural, natural by legal fiction, and spurious

How status is fixed -- birth within a valid marriage, freedom of the parents to marry at conception, later marriage producing legitimation, and acknowledgment -- and the three rights that vary with filiation: the father's surname, support, and succession to his estate

The facts of De Santos v. Angeles: Dr. Antonio de Santos married Sofia Bona in 1941, obtained an unrecognized Nevada divorce in 1949, married Conchita Talag in Tokyo and sired eleven children, then married her validly in Tagaytay on April 23, 1967 after Sofia's death, and died in 1981

The trial court under Judge Adoracion Angeles held Conchita's children legitimated by the Tagaytay marriage and made them coequal heirs with Sofia's lone legitimate child, prompting the certiorari petition

The 8-7 majority through Justice Romero held that 'a natural child by legal fiction cannot rise beyond that to which an acknowledged natural child is entitled,' since such children failed the requisite of being natural children under Article 269 and legitimation is a privilege, not a demandable right

The majority's further point that granting legitimacy would cut the legitimate daughter's share from one fourth of the estate to a proportion equal to each of her eleven half-siblings, and that the law from the outset intended to exclude children of illicit relations

The dissenters -- Justices Vitug, Kapunan and CJP -- relied on Article 89, which gives natural children by legal fiction the same status, rights and obligations as acknowledged natural children, including the Article 270 right to be legitimated by their parents' subsequent marriage

CJP's three-requisite analysis: the child must be natural, recognized by both parents, and the parents must validly marry; a natural child by legal fiction holds the first two from inception under Article 89 and needs only the third, which the 1967 Tagaytay marriage supplied once the first spouse's death ended the bigamous impediment
His distinction between permanent impediments such as incest, which foreclose legitimation forever, and terminable ones such as bigamy, which end with the death of the first spouse

His answer to the prejudice argument: diminution of the legitimate child's share is precisely the effect legitimation produces under Article 272, the legislature having weighed those consequences when it cast 'a mantle of protection upon the children of void marriages,' and the Family Code's repeal of Article 89 cannot impair already vested rights
The second battle: whether a right of first refusal may be enforced by specific performance, answered in Equatorial Realty Development, Inc. and Carmelo & Bauermann, Inc. v. Mayfair Theater

The facts: Carmelo leased to Mayfair for twenty years the Claro M. Recto property where Maxim and Miramar Theaters stood, under lease clauses giving the lessee a '30-days exclusive option to purchase'; after a 1974 telephone overture and Mayfair's reminder of its right, Carmelo sold the whole property to Equatorial in 1978 for P11,300,000

The trial court found the option void for lack of separate consideration; the Court of Appeals and then the Supreme Court through Justice Hermosisima held that the clause created a right of first refusal whose consideration was 'built into the reciprocal obligations of the parties,' rescinded the sale, and let Mayfair buy at P11,300,000

The line-up: eight justices concurred unqualifiedly, Justice Padilla and CJP wrote separate concurrences, Justice Vitug (joined by Justice Torres) dissented, Justice Romero concurred and dissented, and Chief Justice Narvasa took no part

Justice Vitug's dissent that rescission is merely subsidiary, that a breach of the right of first refusal sounds only in damages under Article 19, and that no one can be forced by a court into a contract against his will

CJP's reply: the right sprang from an express covenant with the force of law between the parties, creating a correlative obligation to tender the offer to Mayfair; had Mayfair known in time it could have sued under Articles 1165 and 1191 and enjoined the sale, and its prompt suit for specific performance after learning of the sale amounted to a 'solemn, formal, and unqualified acceptance' of the misdirected offer whose price and terms were already fixed

stances.claim: A natural child by legal fiction is placed by Article 89 on the plane of an acknowledged natural child and therefore needs only the parents' subsequent valid marriage to be legitimated; where the bigamous impediment ended with the first spouse's death, that marriage legitimates the children.
stances.rhetorical_move: statutory integration: reading Articles 89, 269, 270 and 272 together and walking through the three requisites of legitimation one by one

stances.claim: It is unfair to stigmatize children for marital impediments they neither caused nor controlled; in the final analysis there are no illegitimate children, only illegitimate parents, and children should benefit by every intendment of the law.
stances.rhetorical_move: moral reframing that shifts blame from the children to the parents and treats the law's protective policy as the interpretive tiebreaker

stances.claim: That legitimation reduces the legitimate child's share is no objection, because diminution is precisely the effect Article 272 contemplates and the legislature is presumed to have weighed it when it cast a mantle of protection upon the children of void marriages.
stances.rhetorical_move: anticipating and absorbing the opposing consequence by showing it is the statute's design, with a vested-rights backstop against the Family Code's repeal

stances.claim: Although a right of first refusal is normally not enforceable by specific performance, where it is an express contractual covenant, the offer was wrongfully directed to another at a fixed price, and the holder promptly sued for specific performance, consent should be legally presumed and the principle of consensuality deemed satisfied.
stances.rhetorical_move: narrow fact-bound concurrence: conceding the general rule, then constructing acceptance from the aggrieved party's own suit to supply the missing meeting of minds

stances.claim: A breach of a right of first refusal can give rise only to an action for damages under Article 19 and its related provisions, because such a right lacks the indispensable element of consensuality and no one can be forced by a court into a contract against his will.
stances.rhetorical_move: Justice Vitug's dissenting position, quoted as the view CJP answers

notable_anecdotes: The De Santos family history reads like a novel: a 1941 marriage that soured, a doctor falling in love with a fellow physician, a Nevada divorce Philippine law would not recognize, a Tokyo wedding, eleven children, a first wife dying in Guatemala, and a Tagaytay marriage less than a month later.

CJP notes the stake in the arithmetic: instead of one fourth of her father's estate, the lone legitimate daughter would have had to share equally with eleven half-brothers and half-sisters -- the very consequence he said legitimation is designed to produce.

His most quoted line in the chapter comes in defense of children born under impediments they did not create: 'In the final analysis, there are really no illegitimate children; there are only illegitimate parents.'

In Mayfair, the covenant at the center of a multimillion-peso fight was a single sentence in a lease: if the lessor should desire to sell, the lessee 'shall be given 30-days exclusive option to purchase the same.'

He observes that Mayfair never had the chance to enjoin the sale because it learned of the transfer to Equatorial only after it had been consummated -- and that its immediate suit for specific performance is what he treats as its acceptance of the misdirected offer.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' takes up two civil-rights battles fought inside private law. The first is De Santos v. Angeles, on the successional rights of natural children by legal fiction. After a primer on the Civil Code's categories of filiation and the three rights that vary with them -- surname, support and succession -- Justice Panganiban recounts the facts: Dr. Antonio de Santos married Sofia Bona in 1941, secured an unrecognized Nevada divorce in 1949, married Conchita Talag in Tokyo and had eleven children by her, and married her validly in Tagaytay in 1967 after Sofia's death. The trial court treated those children as legitimated and coequal heirs with the lone legitimate daughter, but an 8-7 majority through Justice Romero reversed, holding that 'a natural child by legal fiction cannot rise beyond that to which an acknowledged natural child is entitled' and that legitimation is a privilege, not a demandable right. Dissenting with Justices Vitug and Kapunan, CJP read Article 89 as placing such children on the plane of acknowledged natural children, so that they satisfy the first two requisites of legitimation from inception and need only the parents' subsequent valid marriage -- available here because the bigamous impediment, unlike incest, ended with the first spouse's death. He answered the objection that legitimation would cut the legitimate daughter's share by showing that Article 272 intends exactly that effect, the legislature having cast 'a mantle of protection upon the children of void marriages,' and he defended the children in moral terms: they had no fault in nor control over their parents' impediments, and 'there are really no illegitimate children; there are only illegitimate parents.' The second battle is Equatorial Realty v. Mayfair Theater, where a lease clause giving the lessee a thirty-day exclusive option to purchase was breached by a sale of the Recto property to Equatorial. The Court through Justice Hermosisima treated the clause as a right of first refusal needing no separate consideration, rescinded the sale and let Mayfair buy at P11,300,000. Over Justice Vitug's dissent that such a breach sounds only in damages, CJP concurred separately: the covenant had the force of law, the offer was wrongfully directed to Equatorial at a fixed price, and Mayfair's prompt suit for specific performance was an unqualified acceptance, so consensuality was satisfied.
